title: Circuit Analysis I
full_title: Circuit Analysis I: DC Circuits and Transients
tagline: Circuit laws, network theorems, op-amps and first- and second-order transients
summary: Electric circuits are the language of electrical engineering. This course develops the laws of Ohm and Kirchhoff, systematic nodal and mesh analysis, the network theorems, ideal operational amplifiers, and the transient behaviour of circuits with capacitors and inductors.
overview: Circuits are the skeleton of every electronic device. A **circuit** is a closed path along which charge can flow, and this course gives you the tools to predict exactly what happens in one: the currents, the voltages and the time-dependence, from the first instant a switch is closed until everything settles. We begin with the fundamental physical quantities — charge, current, voltage and power — and the two universal rules, Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws, from which every circuit result follows.

The course then builds the practical methods: reducing resistive networks to a single equivalent element, solving any linear network systematically by nodal and mesh analysis, applying the powerful network theorems (superposition, Thévenin, Norton, maximum power transfer), and using the operational amplifier to realise ideal mathematical operations. Finally we add energy storage through capacitors and inductors, and learn how real circuits behave in time — the natural and forced responses of first- and second-order networks, and how to analyse any of them with a computer.

What makes circuits hard is not any single formula but the discipline of modelling: choosing a consistent sign convention, identifying the independent variables, writing the right equations and checking units and magnitudes. We work toward that discipline throughout, with fully worked examples that show every step, and exercises that take you from routine calculations to design.
outcomes: Model real electronic components as ideal circuit elements and apply the passive sign convention consistently.
Reduce any resistive network to an equivalent resistance, voltage or current divider and solve it exactly.
Set up and solve any linear resistive network by nodal analysis, mesh analysis or a combination of both.
Apply superposition, Thévenin and Norton theorems and maximum power transfer to simplify analysis and guide design.
Analyse circuits containing ideal operational amplifiers and realise summing, difference and integrating transfer functions.
Derive and solve the differential equations governing first- and second-order circuits, including the step, natural and forced responses.
Choose component values so that a circuit meets a given specification, and interpret the results in terms of time constants and damping.
Use a circuit simulator to verify hand analysis and to explore behaviour that is tractable only numerically.

chapters.title: Charge, current, voltage and power
chapters.summary: Electric charge and current, voltage, power and energy, the passive sign convention, and ideal independent and dependent sources.

chapters.title: Resistive circuits
chapters.summary: Ohm’s law, Kirchhoff’s current and voltage laws, series and parallel resistors, and voltage and current dividers.

chapters.title: Nodal and mesh analysis
chapters.summary: Systematic analysis with node voltages and mesh currents, supernodes and supermeshes, and circuits with dependent sources.

chapters.title: Network theorems
chapters.summary: Linearity and superposition, source transformations, Thévenin and Norton equivalents, and maximum power transfer.

chapters.title: Operational amplifiers
chapters.summary: The ideal op-amp model and the inverting, non-inverting, summing, difference and buffer amplifiers.

chapters.title: Capacitors and inductors
chapters.summary: Capacitance and inductance, stored energy, series and parallel combinations, and continuity of capacitor voltage and inductor current.

chapters.title: First-order circuits
chapters.summary: Natural and step responses of RC and RL circuits, time constants, switched circuits and op-amp integrators.

chapters.title: Second-order circuits
chapters.summary: Series and parallel RLC circuits, the characteristic equation, and overdamped, critically damped and underdamped responses.

chapters.title: Computer-aided circuit analysis
chapters.summary: Matrix formulation of circuit equations, modified nodal analysis, and how circuit simulators such as SPICE compute DC and transient solutions.

history.title: Volta's pile
history.detail: The stacking of alternate metal and brined card produced the first steady source of electric current, creating the field in its own right.

history.title: Ohm's law
history.detail: Georg Ohm published Die galvanische Kette, giving the relation between current, voltage and resistance in a quantitative form.

history.title: Kirchhoff's laws
history.detail: Kirchhoff formulated the current and voltage conservation laws, providing the two equations that underlie all network analysis.

history.title: Thévenin's theorem
history.detail: The idea of replacing any linear network by a voltage source and resistance, later generalised by Norton, became a cornerstone of circuit design.

history.title: SPICE
history.detail: The Simulation Program with Integration Circuits appeared at UC Berkeley; it is the ancestor of essentially every circuit simulator used today.

references.title: Fundamentals of Electric Circuits
references.note: The standard first circuits text. Clear worked examples; the first three chapters map directly onto this course.

references.title: Electric Circuits
references.note: A more engineering-oriented treatment with strong emphasis on power and energy. Good for the AC-adjacent material.

references.title: Engineering Circuit Analysis
references.authors: William Hayt, Jack Kemmerly, Stephen Durbin
references.note: Rigorous and comprehensive; a good reference for nodal/mesh and operational amplifier coverage.

references.title: Linear Circuit Analysis
references.note: Short and clear; useful for second-order and transient response intuition.
